title: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play by Jocelyn Bioh on Broa...
transcript: I don't know if there's a more poignant or pointed play about colorism than this one. I missed School Girls when it premiered in 2017, so I was glad to see it come back after the success of Jocelyn Bioh's more recent play about a braiding salon in Harlem. This one has the same level of specificity, but I think it's even more of a complete thought. Set in 1986, it follows a group of girls eager to compete in the Miss Ghana pageant. Queen bee Paulina seems to be a shoo-in for the crown, until Ericka arrives at the school with fairer skin and an American backstory. Pretty much everything about this production is excellent, from the casting and the performances to the impeccable pacing and direction by Whitney White. Denée Benton is gloriously ruthless as Paulina — from her entrance alone, we know exactly who she is before a single line is spoken. The script is marvellously zippy, and it's a blast watching these high schoolers with their claws out. But for how well it succeeds as a crackling comedy about a teenage battleground, it's just as much a searing commentary on the systems that breed it. The themes of social hierarchy, beauty standards and internalized racism ring loud and clear, and the illustration of these themes through the teenage experience make this play especially moving and universal. Don't miss it. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
